text: In recent years, the nucleation behavior of liquids on solid surfaces has garnered significant attention. It is worth noting that the wettability of the wall plays a pivotal role in determining both the nucleation onset and the subsequent bubble growth [cite]. In this section, we delve into the effects of wettability on the nucleation process based on our molecular dynamics simulations.

Fig. [ref] presents the temporal evolution of the vapor fraction near the wall for contact angles of 35$^\circ$, 70$^\circ$ and 110$^\circ$. Our results clearly demonstrate that the hydrophilic surface significantly accelerates nucleation: the onset time decreases from 350 ps on the 110$^\circ$ surface to 125 ps on the 35$^\circ$ surface at a wall temperature of 300 K. Interestingly, the 70$^\circ$ surface exhibits an intermediate onset time of 210 ps, which proves that the onset time varies monotonically with the contact angle.

The trend can be interpreted using classical nucleation theory, as expressed in Eq. [ref], where the energy barrier $\Delta G^*$ decreases on more hydrophilic surfaces due to the enhanced solid--liquid interaction [cite]. This innovative finding sheds light on the intricate interplay between interfacial wettability and phase change, and paves the way for the rational design of high-performance cooling surfaces for next-generation electronic devices.
